title: Trims, trails and scaling out
teaches: We buy the full size at one price with one stop: no starter piece, never an add to a loser, and an add to a working winner is rare, a feel call, never the plan; we scale OUT: the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the stop moved to breakeven after it, and the rest trails a rising average; never average down; and what scaling out costs and what it buys.

walkthroughs.title: Add only to a winner
steps: You can build a position in steps. Each new step comes only after the last one is working.
Adding to a loser is averaging down. O'Neil's advice on that was simple: don't do it.
Every add is a new trade. It gets its own stop and its own size.

walkthroughs.title: What an add does to your numbers
steps: Buy more above your first price and your average cost goes up.
IBD buys fewer shares on an add than on the first buy, so the average doesn't run up too far.
More shares also means a stop-out costs more. Check what the whole position loses at the stop before you add.

walkthroughs.title: Scaling out, and what it costs
steps: You're up nicely on a winner. Scaling out means you sell part of it and let the rest ride.
First sell's a judgment call, rarely before day 3, into a push. Stop can go to breakeven. The rest trails.
It isn't free. On a stock that runs straight to its target, selling half halfway made less than holding it all.
It pays when the stock comes back on you. You gave up some upside for a gain you get to keep.

walkthroughs.title: One price, one stop
steps: We buy the full size at one price, with one stop. No starter piece, and we never add to a loser.
The stop sets the size before the buy. Then it all goes in as one market order.
Adding to a working winner on strength happens, but it's rare and a feel call, never the plan.
What we do scale is the exit. Sell some into strength, rarely before day 3, and trail the rest.

questions.q: A friend bought 200 shares at $40. It's working, so he buys 100 more at $46. What did he just do?
questions.why: He averaged up. He bought more of a stock he already owns, at a higher price than his first buy. That drags his average cost up from $40 toward $46. Plenty of traders press a winner this way as a habit. We don't plan it. Our full size goes on at one price, with one stop, and the size came from that stop. Add above it and a normal pullback now costs more than you planned. Adding to a working winner does happen, but it's rare and a feel call.
questions.lesson_line: Adding above your first buy is averaging up. For us it's rare, never the plan.

wrong.Averaged down on a loser: That's buying more after the price drops below your buy. This one went up.
wrong.Dollar-cost averaged in: That's the same money in on a set schedule, whatever the price. He bought because it was working.
wrong.Scaled out of the trade: Scaling out is selling part. He bought more.

questions.simple: He averaged up, buying more above his first price. We buy the full size once, and an add is rare.

questions.q: A trader buys more of a stock every time it drops below his first buy. That's called pyramiding.
questions.why: False. That's averaging down, the opposite. Pyramiding adds to a stock while it's working, each add smaller than the last. Averaging down adds while it's going against you. It feels like a bargain. Really you're putting more money behind the trade that's proving you wrong. We never average down. The whole size goes on at one price, with one stop. Adding to a winner happens, but it's rare, a feel call.
questions.lesson_line: Pyramiding adds to a winner. Buying the drops is averaging down.
questions.simple: False. Buying as it falls is averaging down, pyramiding adds as it works, and we never average down.

questions.q: Buying more of a red trade because it dropped is the same thing as dollar-cost averaging.
questions.why: False, and don't let the name fool you. Dollar-cost averaging puts the same money in on a set schedule, whatever the price does. Averaging down is buying more because the stock went against you. One's a plan made in advance. The other's a reaction to a loss. On a swing trade, our answer to a red trade is the stop, not more shares.
questions.lesson_line: A schedule is a plan. Buying more of a loser is a reaction.
questions.simple: False. Dollar-cost averaging buys on a set schedule, while averaging down buys because the stock went against you.

reasons: stable definitions, a Tier 1 SEC fact plus Investopedia

questions.q: O'Neil had one line on averaging. What's the missing word?
questions.sentence: The only averaging that makes sense is averaging ___.
questions.why: Up. O'Neil's view on averaging down was simple: don't. He called it throwing good money after bad. The only averaging he'd accept was averaging up, adding to a stock that's proving you right. We buy the full size once, at one price with one stop. No starter piece, no scaling in. Adding to a working winner is rare for us, a feel call, never the plan. The part we share with him matters most: never add to a loser.
questions.lesson_line: Never add to a loser. O'Neil said it, and we live by it.
questions.simple: Up. O'Neil said never average down, and we never add to a loser either.

reasons: the why adds the owner's rule A5 (no adding)

deeper.counter: Hirsch makes the same point from the other side: he lists averaging down into losing positions among the deadly sins of managing positions.

questions.q: Adding to a winner at a higher price raises your average cost per share.
questions.why: True. Every share you buy above your average pulls the average up. IBD keeps adds smaller than the first buy so it doesn't run up too far.
questions.lesson_line: Adds raise your average cost. Keep them small so it stays close to your first buy.

questions.q: You sell part of a winner into strength and keep the rest on, with a stop under it. What's that called?
questions.why: Scaling out. You close the trade in pieces instead of all at once. The piece you sell puts a gain in your pocket. The rest stays on for the bigger move, with a stop that rises behind it. That's how we hold winners. Our first sell is a judgment, and we very rarely make it before day 3. Then the rest trails the 9 or 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some, let the rest ride. That's scaling out.

wrong.Stopping out of it: That's your stop getting hit. A stop-out isn't a planned sale into a gain.
wrong.Averaging down on it: That's buying more after a drop. You sold here.
wrong.Pyramiding into it: Pyramiding adds shares to a winner. You took shares off.

questions.simple: Scaling out. You sell part of a winner and let the rest ride with a stop behind it.

questions.q: One line sums up how we hold a winner. What's the missing word?
questions.sentence: Hold your winners by selling partials into ___ and trailing the rising moving averages.
questions.why: Strength. You sell part while the stock is still pushing higher and looks great to everyone. That's when buyers are there to take your shares. Wait until it rolls over and you're selling into weakness, with everyone else heading for the door. It feels wrong to sell a stock that's working. Do it anyway, then trail the rest under the rising averages.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into strength, trail the rest. Don't wait for it to roll over.
questions.simple: Strength. We sell part while the stock is rising and buyers are there, then trail the rest under the rising averages.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule (sizing_rule.md section 6, A11)

deeper.counter: IBD says the best way to sell is while the stock is on the way up and looks strong to everyone, and admits that runs contrary to human nature. O'Neil taught the same timing.

questions.q: You own 300 shares at $40. You add 100 shares at $44. What's your new average cost per share?
questions.why: $41. The 100-share add is a third the size of your first buy, so your average only moves a little toward $44.
questions.lesson_line: A small add barely moves your average cost. That's why IBD keeps adds smaller than the first buy.

questions.q: Your trade's working and you're thinking about taking some off. What decides when that first sell goes in?
choices: A third at 3R, every single time
Half of it once the stock doubles
questions.why: Judgment. There's no fixed price for it, and I won't pretend there is. I very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. Day 3 is the earliest I'd look at it most of the time. The spot I like is into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or somewhere around 5 to 10R. How the stock's acting decides it. R is just the ruler, your entry minus your stop.
questions.lesson_line: First sell: a judgment, usually day 3 or later. R is the ruler, not the trigger.

wrong.A third at 3R, every single time: That's a formula. Our first sell is a judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push.
wrong.Half of it once the stock doubles: Some traders sell half on a double. We don't wait on a fixed number like that.
wrong.Some once it's up 20% to 25%: That's IBD's profit-taking zone. We go by how the trade is acting, not a set percent.

questions.simple: Judgment, not a fixed price. It rarely comes before day 3, and how the stock acts into a push decides it.

questions.q: Your full plan is 400 shares, stop $2 under entry. You start with 100 and the stop hits before you add. What do you lose?
questions.why: $200, if it fills at your stop. Only the 100-share starter was on, not the full 400. The flip side: if it runs at once, you own less of the move.
questions.lesson_line: Start small and the trade has to prove itself before your full size is on.

questions.q: Once your trade shows a profit, an add on top of it carries no real risk.
questions.why: False. An add is a whole new setup with its own risk. If the stock turns, the new shares lose, and they can eat the gain on your first shares.
questions.lesson_line: A profit on your first shares doesn't protect the new ones.

questions.story: You bought at $50 with your stop at $48.50, just under the low of the day. It's $49 now and still sliding. A friend says buy more to lower your average.
questions.q: What's your move?
choices: Stick to the stop, add nothing
Hold, but drop the stop to $47
questions.answer: Stick to the stop, add nothing
questions.why: Stick to the stop and add nothing. The stock is proving you wrong, and buying more puts more money behind being wrong. Sure, more shares at $49 lower your average. They also make you bigger in a stock that's falling. If $48.50 goes, you're out. That's the loss you planned when you bought at $50, and it's small. Our stop only moves up, never down.
questions.lesson_line: Never add to a loser. The stop is the plan.

wrong.Buy more, it's cheaper now: Cheaper isn't better. You can't tell a dip from the start of a bigger drop, and more shares make that drop cost more.
wrong.Hold, but drop the stop to $47: That widens the loss you planned. Our stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Buy more right at $48.50: If $48.50 breaks you're out anyway, now with more shares and a bigger loss.

questions.simple: Add nothing and let the stop do its job. Buying more puts more money behind a trade that's proving you wrong.

deeper.trap: The friend's math is right: more shares at $49 do lower your average. That's the trap. A lower average only helps if the stock turns back up. You can't tell a dip from the start of a bigger drop, and the extra shares make that drop cost more. O'Neil called averaging down throwing good money after bad.

questions.q: You bought 100 shares at $50. It drops to $40 and you buy 100 more. Where's your breakeven now?
questions.why: $45. Half your shares cost $50 and half cost $40, so your average sits right in the middle. That's the trap of averaging down. The bar to get back to even dropped. But now twice the shares ride on a stock that's been falling, so every dollar lower costs you double. We'd have been out long before $40, at our stop. That's why we never end up here.
questions.lesson_line: Averaging down lowers the bar and doubles the bet. The stock still has to turn.
questions.simple: $45, right between $50 and $40. But now you hold twice the shares in a falling stock.

wrong.$50.00: That's your first price. The second buy pulled the average down.
wrong.$40.00: That's only the second buy. The average counts both.
wrong.$90.00: You added the two prices and forgot to divide by two.

questions.q: You just sold part of a winner into a strong push. What's the plan for the shares you kept?
choices: Let them ride on a trailing stop
Keep the original stop under them
Buy more on the next dip
Hold them with no stop at all
questions.answer: Let them ride on a trailing stop
questions.why: Let them ride on a trailing stop. The sale put a gain in your pocket, and the rest is there for the bigger move. Now protect it. The stop can come up to breakeven at the first sell. Then the rest trails the 9 EMA on a fast mover or the 20 EMA on a steadier one. A close below the line sells it.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some, then trail the rest. The stop rises as the stock does.

wrong.Keep the original stop under them: On a winner that stop sits way below. Bring it up to breakeven at the first sell, and a reversal costs you far less.
wrong.Buy more on the next dip: Adding isn't the plan. You just sold some into strength. The shares you kept have one job: ride the trail.
wrong.Hold them with no stop at all: A winner can still turn on you. The rest needs a stop that rises with it.

questions.simple: Let them ride on a trailing stop. Bring it up to breakeven, then trail the rising average.

deeper.counter: Hirsch's version: harvest gains, then set trailing stops on what's left.

questions.q: You own 100 shares from $30. It's doubled to $60, and you want your money off the table. How many shares do you sell?
questions.why: 50 shares. Your cost was 100 shares at $30. At $60 every share is worth twice what you paid. So half of them, 50 shares, brings back the whole amount. Now you can't lose your own money on this trade, only some of the gain. Some traders sell half on a double for exactly that reason. We pick the first sell by judgment, but this is handy math to have.
questions.lesson_line: On a double, half the shares pay you back. The rest rides on profit.
questions.simple: 50 shares. At $60 each share is worth twice what you paid, so selling half gets your whole cost back.

wrong.100 shares: That sells everything. At $60 you only need half the shares to get your cost back.
wrong.30 shares: You used the $30 price as a share count.
wrong.25 shares: You halved it twice. Half the shares, not a quarter, return the cost.

questions.q: Your stop sits at breakeven on the shares you kept. A bad gap down can still hand you a loss on them.
questions.why: True. A stop order only names the price where the sale starts. Once it's hit, it becomes a market order and fills at whatever's there. If the stock opens well under your entry, you're starting the day with a loss on those shares. Our gap rule lets the first half hour set a new stop, but it can't put you back above your entry. It's rare, but it happens. That's why a tight stop never licenses a monster position.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven on paper isn't breakeven in a gap.
questions.simple: True. A gap can open below your breakeven stop, so those shares start the day at a loss.

deeper.trap: Breakeven on paper is not breakeven in a gap. A stop order at your entry only names the price that starts the sale. If the stock opens below it, the market order fills at whatever the market pays at that moment.

reasons: Tier 1 FINRA quote reconfirmed on its page 2026-11-12

questions.q: Entry $40, stop $38. Our plans put the first trim at 2R. What price is that?
questions.why: $44. One R is your entry minus your stop. Two of those above your $40 entry is the first trim.
questions.lesson_line: Trims are measured from your own risk. Know the 2R price before you buy.

questions.q: You bought 100 at $50, stop $48. At $55 you add 100 and leave the stop at $48. What does the whole position lose at the stop?
questions.why: $900, if it fills at $48. The add from $55 rides all the way down to $48 too. Leaving the stop where it was turned a small risk into a big one.
questions.lesson_line: Before you add, check what the whole position loses at the stop, not just the new shares.

questions.story: You buy 200 shares at $10. You sell 100 at $12.50 and the last 100 at $15. A friend buys 200 at $10 and sells all of them at $15.
questions.q: Leaving out commissions, who came out ahead?

args.expr: s * (top - entry) - h * (part - entry) - h * (top - entry)

questions.why: Your friend, by $250. He made $5 a share on all 200 shares. You made $5 on only 100 of yours. Your other 100 earned $2.50 and stopped earning at $12.50. When a stock runs all the way, scaling out leaves money on the table. That's the price of a gain in hand, and I'm fine paying it.
questions.lesson_line: Scaling out gives up some of a big run. That's the price of a gain in hand.

wrong.Your friend, by $500: That's double the gap. Only your first 100 shares sold early, at $12.50.
wrong.You did, by selling early: Backwards. Selling early capped the gain on half your shares.
wrong.The same profit for both: Only if you'd sold both halves at $15. You sold one at $12.50.

questions.simple: Your friend made $250 more. Your first 100 shares stopped earning at $12.50 while his kept going to $15.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging scaling out by this one ending. Here the stock ran all the way, so the partial cost you. A trade that turns back first is a different story, so scaling out is a trade-off, not free profit. Bulkowski's first test found the same.

questions.story: You own a winner that broke out a few weeks ago. It's pulling back toward its 50-day moving average. Today it's still falling, on rising volume.
questions.q: You want to add. When do you buy?
choices: After it bounces and turns up
Buy the dip while it's falling
Add today with a wider stop
Double up to catch the low
questions.answer: After it bounces and turns up
questions.why: After it bounces and turns up. IBD's rule: never buy a stock as it's moving down. IBD also wants light volume on a pullback, and this one is on rising volume.
questions.lesson_line: Add on strength, never into a falling stock.

wrong.Buy the dip while it's falling: That's buying weakness. Wait for the stock to show strength first.
wrong.Add today with a wider stop: A wider stop makes the add riskier, and the stock is still falling.
wrong.Double up to catch the low: Nobody can call the low. Doubling up before the turn is a guess, sized big.

questions.story: You own 100 shares from $50. It runs to $56 and pulls back. You add 100 at $55 and raise the stop on all 200 to $52.
questions.q: If the stop fills at $52, where does the whole trade end?
questions.why: A $100 loss. Your first 100 shares make money at $52, but the add from $55 loses more. With your first buy still close to the new stop, a stop-out turns the whole trade red.
questions.lesson_line: Before you add, check where the whole position ends if the new stop hits.

wrong.A $200 gain: That counts only your first 100 shares. The add loses money at $52.
wrong.A $300 loss: That counts only the add. Your first 100 shares are in profit at $52.
wrong.Break even: The two lots don't offset here. The add loses more than the first buy makes.

questions.story: You buy 200 shares at $10. It runs to $12.50 and you sell 100. Then it falls back, and your breakeven stop sells the other 100 at $10.
questions.q: Compared with holding all 200 to that stop, what did the partial do for you?

args.expr: h * (part - entry) + h * (stop - entry) - s * (stop - entry)

questions.why: It made you $250 more. Hold all 200 and the whole trade round-trips to nothing at $10. The partial took $2.50 a share on 100 shares before the stock came back. That's the only money this trade made. Scaling out costs you when a stock runs all the way. It pays you when the stock comes back. You won't know which one you've got, so I like a gain in hand.
questions.lesson_line: Partials pay when the stock comes back. That's what the upside you give up buys you.

wrong.Made no difference: Holding all 200 made nothing. Your partial at $12.50 was real money.
wrong.Made you $500 more: Only 100 shares sold at $12.50, not all 200.
wrong.Left you worse off: Backwards. The partial is the only profit in this trade.

questions.simple: It made you $250 more. Holding all 200 to the $10 stop made nothing, while the partial banked a gain.

deeper.trap: Two things hide here. Bulkowski's third test found the same thing, and his own numbers include commissions, which is why his gain is $220. And a breakeven stop order is not a promise. Once triggered it fills at market, so a gap through $10 could turn the last 100 shares into a loss.

questions.story: You own 200 shares from $40. It's at $50 and a new setup fires there, with its own stop at $47. You risk $300 per trade.
questions.q: What's the most the add can be?
questions.why: 100 shares. The add is a new trade, so it gets sized from its own stop: $300 of risk over the distance from $50 to $47.
questions.lesson_line: An add gets its own stop and its own size, like any new trade.

wrong.200 shares: That copies your first buy. From this stop it risks double your plan.
wrong.300 shares: That reads your risk dollars as shares. It risks three times your plan.
wrong.None, you already own it: Owning it isn't the test. A new buy point in a winner is a chance to add.

questions.story: Your swing trade is well under your entry and close to your stop. You already bought more once on the way down. You still like the company and want to buy more.
questions.q: Which move fits our plan?
choices: Take the loss and move on
Lower the stop, give it room
Buy more, half size this time
questions.answer: Take the loss and move on
questions.why: Take the loss and move on. Bulkowski's line for swing traders: if you want to average down a second time, sell the loser instead. O'Neil and Hirsch say don't average down at all. Our plan never adds, and the stop only moves up. Your first add already made this position bigger than you planned.
questions.lesson_line: Admit the mistake, take the loss, move on. Liking the company doesn't change the chart.

wrong.Average down one more time: That's the second average down Bulkowski says to swap for a sale. If it keeps falling, the loss gets bigger.
wrong.Lower the stop, give it room: Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. Lowering it widens the loss you planned.
wrong.Buy more, half size this time: Smaller is still adding to a loser. The size doesn't fix the direction.

questions.simple: Take the loss and move on. A second buy on the way down only makes a losing trade bigger.

deeper.trap: Under our rule this trade went wrong at the first add, because we never add. Selling now, or letting the stop take it, both end the trade. The two moves our rule forbids are the ones that feel kindest: buying again and giving the stop room.

reasons: asks what fits our plan (A4, A5)

questions.story: You hold a full position in a leader. It's run hard for two weeks and sits way above its rising averages. Your stop is far below.
questions.q: What's the play here?
choices: Lower the stop for more room
Sell it all, it can't go higher
questions.why: Sell some, trail the rest. Two weeks of hard running, way above its averages: that's a stock stretched into strength. Buyers are there, so it's a good time to sell some. You lock in part of the run and keep shares on in case it keeps going. Bring the stop up behind it and trail the rest under the rising averages. You never have to guess the top.
questions.lesson_line: When it's stretched, sell some into strength. Let the rest show you how far it can go.

wrong.Add more while it's running: Not into a stretch like this. Buying a stock this extended is chasing, the kind of buy a normal pullback shakes out.
wrong.Lower the stop for more room: Our stop only moves up, never down. On a winner, lowering it just hands back more of the gain.
wrong.Sell it all, it can't go higher: That's a bet on the top. Sell some into strength and let the trail decide the rest.

questions.simple: Sell some into the strength and trail the rest. You bank part of the run and keep shares on for more.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading 'extended' as a signal to buy more or to sell everything. For us it's neither. A stretched stock is a place to sell some into strength. Hirsch cuts to a two-thirds or even one-third position when a stock is extended short term, and Schwab says sell a portion and let the remainder ride.

questions.q: We buy the whole position at one price, with one stop. Adding to a winner later is rare, and never part of the plan.
questions.why: True. The full size goes on at one price, with one stop. No starter piece, no scaling in. Here's why. The size came from the stop. Your entry minus your stop set how many shares fit the risk you chose. Adding to a working winner on strength does happen, but it's rare and a feel call. Never planned, and never to a loser. We scale the exit, not the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Full size, one price, one stop. We scale out, not in.
questions.simple: True. The stop set the size, so it goes on once, and adding to a winner is rare, a feel call.

questions.q: The trade's moving your way, and your stop still sits under the entry day's low. When does it come up to breakeven?
choices: Between 2R and 5R, or the first sell
The day after you buy, no matter what
Never, the stop stays where it is
As soon as it's 1R in your favor
questions.answer: Between 2R and 5R, or the first sell
questions.why: Somewhere between 2R and 5R, or when you make the first sell. That's a judgment, not one fixed number. Move it too soon, at 1R, and a normal wiggle takes you out of a good trade for nothing. Give it real room first. Once it's at breakeven, the trade can't turn into a real loser short of a gap. From there the stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Give it room first. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

wrong.The day after you buy, no matter what: A date isn't the signal. Give the trade room first, 2R to 5R or the first sell.
wrong.As soon as it's 1R in your favor: Too tight, too soon. One normal pullback and you're out at breakeven on a good trade.
wrong.Never, the stop stays where it is: Our stop never moves down, but it does move up. Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R or the first sell.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. Too soon and a normal wiggle shakes you out of a good trade.

reasons: fixed in final check: key is B19's own window, not the 3R course convention

questions.q: Finish our trim rule.
questions.sentence: At 3R we sell a ___ of the position.
questions.why: A third. Our hard rule is a third at 3R, another third at 5R, and the last third trails a rising average. Ideally the first trim sits anywhere from 3R to 6R. The rule we teach is the hard one: a third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, trail the rest.
questions.simple: A third. At 3R we sell one third, at 5R another third, and the last third trails.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: Your setup triggers. You put in a limit order at the trigger price so you don't pay a cent more than planned.
questions.why: False. We buy at market. When it triggers, I want to be in, and a market order gets me in. A limit at the trigger can sit there unfilled while the stock runs away without you. Then you're either chasing it or you've missed it. The order that waits is the stop: a real stop order with the broker, never one kept in your head.
questions.lesson_line: Entries at market. The stop is the order that waits.
questions.simple: False. We enter at market so we're in when it triggers, and the stop is the order that waits.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, D41)

questions.q: You buy at $50 with your stop at $47.50. Where's 3R on this trade?
questions.why: $57.50. One R is your risk per share: $50 minus $47.50 is $2.50. Three of those is $7.50. Add that to your $50 entry and you're at $57.50. Mark it before you buy. It's a ruler, not a sell order. It tells you how much the trade has paid you for the risk you took. The first sell is still judgment, and rarely before day 3.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R price before you buy. It's a mark on the ruler, not a sell order.
questions.simple: $57.50. Take three times your risk from $50 down to $47.50 and add it to the $50 entry.

wrong.$55.00: That's only 2R. You need three times the $2.50 risk.
wrong.$42.50: You went three R below the entry. 3R sits above it.
wrong.$53.00: You added a flat $3. 3R is three times your risk, not $3.

questions.q: Entry $80, stop $77, and the stock keeps running. Where does 5R sit?
questions.why: $95. Your risk is $80 minus $77, $3 a share. Five R is $15. Add it to $80 and you're at $95. Around 5R is often a good place to sell some, more so into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. But it's a mark, not an order. Whatever you keep trails, so a big winner can keep going.
questions.lesson_line: 5R is a mark on the ruler, not a sell order. The sell is a judgment.
questions.simple: $95. Five times your risk from $80 down to $77, added to the $80 entry, puts 5R there.

wrong.$98.00: That's six times the $3 risk, not five.
wrong.$110.00: You counted the risk twice over. One R here is $3.
wrong.$400.00: That's five times the entry. R is your risk, the $3 between entry and stop.

questions.q: You've sold some and the rest is trailing. Which line do you trail, and what gets you out?
choices: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA
Any dip at all under the 50-day
A 10% drop from the highest price
questions.answer: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA
questions.why: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA. Use the 9 EMA on a fast mover and the 20 EMA on a steadier one. A dip under the line during the day doesn't sell. A close below it does. Leaders shake out intraday all the time, and the close tells you if buyers stepped back in. Put both EMAs on your daily chart so the line is always in front of you.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the 9 or 20 EMA. A close below it sells what's left.

wrong.Any dip at all under the 50-day: Wrong line and wrong signal. Our trail is the 9 or 20 EMA, and it takes a close below, not a dip.
wrong.A close under the 200-day line: By then you've handed back most of the move. We trail the 9 or 20 EMA.
wrong.A 10% drop from the highest price: That's a percent trail. Ours follows a moving average, the 9 or 20 EMA.

questions.simple: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA. A dip during the day doesn't count, the close does.

questions.story: You bought at $20 with your stop at $19. By noon the same day it's $23 on news. That's already 3R.
questions.q: Do you make your first sell?
choices: Hold, we rarely sell on day 1
Sell a third now, it's at 3R
Sell it all, a gain is a gain
Sell half now and lift the stop
questions.answer: Hold, we rarely sell on day 1
questions.why: Hold. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. You risked $1 a share from $20 to $19, and by noon you're up $3. That's a stock telling you it wants to go. Selling into it caps your best trade on its first day. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest, and a 3, 5 or 7 day push is often where the first sell goes.
questions.lesson_line: We rarely sell on day 1. Let a strong stock show you what it's got.

wrong.Sell it all, a gain is a gain: That cuts your best trade short on its first day. Let it show you what it's got.
wrong.Sell half now and lift the stop: Day 1 is too early. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.Sell a third now, it's at 3R: 3R is a mark, not a sell order. And we rarely sell on day 1.

questions.simple: Hold, we very rarely sell on day 1 and wait for day 3 or later, into a push.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, B19)

questions.story: You bought a setup 11 trading days ago. It never came near the stop, but it's up only about half an R and going nowhere.
questions.q: What's the call here?
choices: Sell it, the time stop hit
Move the stop up to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it, the time stop hit
questions.why: Sell it. That's our time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold. This one's at half an R on day 11, so it goes. Dead money has a cost even when it never hits the stop. That money could be in a stock that's moving. If it sets up again later, you can buy it again as a new trade.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after 10 trading days: sell. Dead money has a cost.

wrong.Hold until the stop or 3R: 3R isn't an exit we wait for. And under 1R after 10 trading days, the time stop ends it.
wrong.Widen the stop and wait: The stop never moves down or wider. And waiting is the problem here, not the fix.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R. This trade is under 1R, so the time stop sells it.

questions.simple: Sell it. It's gone 11 days without real progress, so the time stop frees the money for a stock that's moving.

deeper.trap: The trap is that nothing looks wrong. The stop never hit and the trade is green. But the time stop measures progress, not losses. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, so the money can go to a setup that's moving.

questions.q: Your stock gaps down through your stop at the open. The low of the first 30-minute bar becomes your new stop.
questions.why: True. That's our gap rule. Rather than dump it into the opening panic, you let the first 30 minutes show you where it holds. Their low becomes the new stop. There's a ceiling: if those 30 minutes already put the loss past 2R, you get out. It's the one time a stop moves down. Every other time it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop. Past 2R, you're out.
questions.simple: True. On a gap through your stop, the first 30 minutes decide, and their low is your new stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, G70)
open question for the owner: how the broker stop order (D41) meets the gap rule

questions.story: You bought your full size at $30, stop $28.50. Two days later it's at $33, and a friend says add half again, it's working.
questions.q: Do you add?
choices: Add half, it's proving you right
Add half, raise the stop on all
Sell it all and rebuy bigger
questions.why: Add nothing. You put the full size on at $30, with one stop at $28.50, and that stop set your size. Add half at $33 and your average climbs. A pullback to $30 now costs you on the new shares. Adding to a working winner does happen, but it's rare and a feel call, never the plan. Manage what you have instead. At $33 you're twice your risk ahead, so a breakeven stop is now on the table.
questions.lesson_line: Full size at one price. Then you manage it. An add is rare, never the plan.

wrong.Add half, it's proving you right: Working isn't reason enough on its own. Your job now is managing what you have, not growing it.
wrong.Add half, raise the stop on all: Raising the stop is fine. The add isn't. More shares bought higher raise what a reversal costs.
wrong.Sell it all and rebuy bigger: That's an add with extra steps. Our size was set from the stop at the entry.

questions.simple: Add nothing. Your size went on once, from the stop, and buying more higher raises what a pullback costs.

deeper.counter: Averaging up is a real method. IBD uses later buy points to add to a position it already holds. We don't plan a trade that way. Our size is set once, from the stop at the entry, so the risk you planned is the risk you carry.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, B19)

questions.story: You bought 300 shares at $40, stop $38. By day 5 it's run to $46, a strong 5 day push, well above its rising 9 EMA.
questions.q: What's the plan now?
choices: Sell some at $46, trail the rest
Hold all 300 and never sell a share
questions.answer: Sell some at $46, trail the rest
questions.why: Sell some at $46 and trail the rest. Your risk was $2 a share, $40 minus $38. At $46 you're up $6, 3R. That alone isn't the reason. The 5 day push is. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push is often best, and this is that spot. The rest rides the rising 9 EMA and sells on a close below it. How much to sell is your call.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into the push. Trail the rest.

wrong.Sell all 300 at $46, one target: That banks everything at one price. Sell some into strength and trail the rest.
wrong.Hold all 300 and never sell a share: That banks nothing into a 5 day push. Sell some into strength and trail the rest.
wrong.Add 100 more shares at $46: Not into a 5 day push this stretched. That's where we sell some, not where we buy more.

questions.simple: Sell some at $46 into the 5 day push and trail the rest under the rising 9 EMA.

deeper.example: Count it in R. $46 is 3R, a mark and not a sell order. The first sell is a judgment into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R. The rest has no target: it rides the 9 EMA until a close below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51, E52)

conflicts: Shape of the ladder. IBD (s1: add-ons are 'fewer shares than you purchased in the initial breakout') and IBKR (s11: 'successively smaller increments') put the biggest piece first; Investopedia (s7) starts with smaller trade sizes and adds when winning; Bulkowski (s14) says 'I do not buy half a position and then buy another half. I buy a full position' and on a fresh breakout 'I'll double my position.' docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 5 ('Progressive exposure: pilot, half, full, add only after the last step paid') is not marked as the owner's answer or quoted in his words, so it is a lead, not a house source. The file keys only what all of them agree on: add only to a trade that is working, never to a loser; size each add as a new trade; IBD's stated reason for a smaller add (it keeps the average cost down). Settled by the owner, 2026-11-09 (sizing_rule.md section 5 and rule A5): 'I do not scale into trade i buy full at one spot with one stop.' No ladder on the way in is taught as ours; every item that built a position in pieces or added to one is cut (w1, w2, q05, q08, q10, q11, q18, q20, q21, q23).

Investopedia 'Scale In' (s7) contradicts itself: its definition and first example describe buying as the price falls ($20, $19.90, $19.80, $19.70 for a $19.85 average), which is scale trading or averaging down, while its Benefits section describes starting small and adding only when the trade is winning. The file cites only the Benefits lines (f19, f20) and the scale-out lines (f21, f22), and never keys a definition of 'scaling in'.

Does scaling out pay? Bulkowski (s12) and the Howard Bandy study he reports (Active Trader, September 2009) find scaling out lowers profit on trades that run; Dave Mabe, in a third-party post on IBKR Campus ('Exiting Your Trades: What Works Best?', 2025-01-31), says he doesn't scale out 'since you end up paying for the privilege with trading profit'. Schwab (s6), Fidelity / Hirsch (s4), Investopedia (s7, s8) and the owner's own rule (h01) favour selling part into strength. The file teaches it as a trade-off with both halves sourced and calculated (q19: less when the stock runs to target; q22: more when it comes back), never as more profit. The Mabe post is not cited (a third-party blog repost IBKR disclaims).

Bandy's scaling-in study (reported on s14): in a flat 2004 to 2008 market with month-long holds, averaging down ($264 a trade) beat every other test except buy-and-hold with no stops ($1,810). Bulkowski takes issue (gaps, one neutral market). The file never claims averaging down always loses; it keys O'Neil's and Hirsch's rule and the mechanics (a lower average on a bigger position in a falling stock, which still has to turn up).

Bulkowski (s13) allows a swing trader ONE average down when the market and industry are rising, and says sell instead of a second. O'Neil (s3) and Hirsch (s4) say don't average down at all. The file's scenarios key 'don't add' only where all three agree: a stock sliding toward the stop (q12) or a second average down (q24).

Breakeven stops.
